183.title: Sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:30–44)
183.hook: he looks at the crowd with compassion and feeds five thousand
183.howItsDone: Many Christians connect the feeding of the five thousand with communion, where bread is blessed, broken and given, and churches often run food banks and shared meals with this story in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John's head: a ruler's oath at a feast, and a good man killed for it. Your line was careless words cost lives. Which promise did you keep? Day one hundred eighty-three.

The twelve come back from their travels, full of stories, and exhausted. So many people are coming and going that they don't even have time to eat. You know that week. Jesus says, come away with me to a quiet place and rest a while. They get in the boat. And the crowd sees where they're headed and runs around the shore on foot, and gets there first. The boat lands, and there they are. Thousands. Your day off, gone. Most of us would sigh. Mark tells us what Jesus felt instead. Today: sheep without a shepherd.
screen: `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `COME AWAY AND REST.` → `THE CROWD GETS THERE FIRST.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: Jesus "saw much people, and was moved with compassion toward them, because they were as sheep not having a shepherd." Moved with compassion is a gut word in Greek. It comes from the word for your insides. He felt it in his stomach. And sheep without a shepherd is an old phrase in Israel's scriptures, for a people with no one to guide or protect them. So he teaches them, for hours. Then it's late, in the middle of nowhere, and the disciples do the sensible thing: send them away to buy food. And Jesus says four words: "Give ye them to eat." You give them something. They do the math out loud. Two hundred days' wages wouldn't cover it. He asks, what have you got? Five loaves and two fish. He has everyone sit in groups on the green grass. Only Mark says green, which may point to spring. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the bread, and gives it to the disciples to hand out. Take, bless, break, give: Christians hear those same four actions again at the Last Supper, and at the communion table today. Everyone eats and is satisfied. And the leftovers fill twelve baskets. Some readers smile that there is one for each disciple who said send them away. About five thousand men, Mark says; Matthew adds, besides women and children. Christians have read it as a miracle of Jesus's power and a picture of God feeding his people. Many also notice what he did with the disciples: he didn't let them off the hook. He started with their little and put it in their hands.
screen: `MOVED WITH COMPASSION.` · `GIVE YE THEM TO EAT.` · `TAKE, BLESS, BREAK, GIVE.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see a crowd with compassion. Settle, and breathe. Picture a crowd you'll be part of today. A commute, a store, a feed full of strangers, a waiting room. Usually we see crowds as obstacles. Try seeing them the way the text says Jesus did. Every face tired. Every face hungry for something. Many with no one looking out for them. Let the feeling land in your gut. If you pray, you can pray for that crowd. Then ask what little you have that could go into someone's hands. The bell holds the time.
Sheep without a shepherd. How Jesus saw a crowd that ruined his day off: not a nuisance, but people with no one to care for them.
Your line: you give them something. Today, when you're tempted to send a need away, see what little you have and give it. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: It is I (Mark 6:45–52)
184.hook: walking on the lake at night: take heart, it is I, do not be afraid
184.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to this story in times of fear or long struggle, and the words be of good cheer, it is I, be not afraid are often read at services for the sick and the grieving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a crowd like sheep without a shepherd, and five loaves in the disciples' hands. Your line was you give them something. What little did you give? Day one hundred eighty-four.

Straight after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples off in the boat ahead of him, sends the crowd home, and climbs a hill alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the lake, the wind turns against them. They row, and row, and get nowhere. Hours of it. Arms burning, the shore not getting any closer. You know that kind of night, even if you've never held an oar: a problem you've been rowing against since sundown. And then, somewhere between three and six in the morning, someone sees a figure on the water. Walking. Today: it is I.
screen: `ALONE ON THE HILL TO PRAY.` → `ROWING AGAINST THE WIND.` → `A FIGURE ON THE WATER.`

segments.voice: In the old King James Bible: "he saw them toiling in rowing; for the wind was contrary unto them: and about the fourth watch of the night he cometh unto them, walking upon the sea, and would have passed by them." He saw them. From the hill, in the dark, he's been watching them struggle. The fourth watch is the last stretch of the night, before dawn. And then a strange phrase: he would have passed by them. Readers have puzzled over it. Many hear an echo of the old stories where God passes by Moses on the mountain and Elijah at the cave, showing himself as he goes. The disciples think it's a ghost, and they scream. And he speaks at once: "Be of good cheer: it is I; be not afraid." Take heart. It is I. Don't be afraid. In Greek, it is I is two words, ego eimi, which can also mean simply, I am. Many Christians hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush: I am. Then he climbs into the boat, and the wind stops. You might expect joy. Mark gives us something more honest: they were utterly astonished, "For they considered not the miracle of the loaves: for their heart was hardened." They'd just seen five thousand fed, and it hadn't sunk in. Mark keeps showing us disciples who don't quite get it, which is comforting for anyone who doesn't either. And Mark's version has no Peter stepping out onto the water. That's in Matthew. Here it's just Jesus, the dark, the wind, and three phrases for frightened people: take heart, it is I, don't be afraid.
screen: `HE SAW THEM TOILING IN ROWING.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY THEM.` · `IT IS I — EGO EIMI, I AM.` · `THEIR HEART WAS HARDENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say take heart to someone. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone rowing against the wind right now. A friend with a long night behind them and more ahead. Someone whose arms are tired. Hold them in mind. Imagine standing near them and saying, simply, take heart. You're not alone in this. If you pray, you can pray the words from the story for them: be of good cheer, be not afraid. Then choose how you'll actually say it today: a message, a call, a note. The bell holds the time.
It is I. What Jesus says to frightened men in a boat before dawn. In Greek, ego eimi, which can also mean I am.
Your line: take heart, it is I. Today, say take heart to one person who's rowing against the wind. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: Wherever he went (Mark 6:53–56)
185.hook: villages lay the sick in the marketplaces just to touch his fringe
185.howItsDone: Many Christians bring the needs of others into prayer by name, alone or aloud in church, and many congregations keep prayer lists for the sick of their community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a figure on the water before dawn, and three phrases: take heart. It is I. Don't be afraid. Who did you say take heart to? Day one hundred eighty-five.

The boat lands at Gennesaret, a fertile plain on the lake's western shore. The moment Jesus steps out, someone recognizes him. And then it's like watching news spread before phones. People run through the whole region. Anyone with someone sick at home picks them up, mat and all, and carries them to wherever they've heard he is. Village, town, farm, it doesn't matter. Today is just four verses long. No big speech, no single story. A snapshot of what it was like. Today: wherever he went.

Here's the last verse, in the old King James Bible: "And whithersoever he entered, into villages, or cities, or country, they laid the sick in the streets, and besought him that they might touch if it were but the border of his garment: and as many as touched him were made whole." The streets here are the marketplaces, the open squares at the heart of every town. Picture the busiest square you know, lined with people on mats, waiting. And what do they ask for? Not a speech. Not even a word. Just to touch the border of his garment. Remember the woman in the crowd, a week ago. What she did in secret, a whole region now does in the open. The border, in Greek, is kraspedon, a fringe or tassel. The law of Moses told the people of Israel to wear tassels on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue, to remember God's commandments. Many Jews still wear them today, called tzitzit. So the fringe they reached for was very likely one of those: Jesus dressed as an observant Jew, and the sick reaching for the reminder of God's commands on his clothes. And with that, the second part of Mark closes. Seeds, storms and loaves. The sower from a boat. Why parables. A lamp on a stand. Seed growing secretly. Asleep on a cushion. Legion. Go home and tell. The hem of his garment. Talitha koum. The carpenter at home. Travel light. John's head. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I. And now, wherever he went. Next, Mark asks the question straight out: who is this?
screen: `WHITHERSOEVER HE ENTERED.` · `THE SICK LAID IN THE STREETS.` · `KRASPEDON — A FRINGE, A TASSEL.` · `SEEDS, STORMS AND LOAVES: DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone's need into prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who carried their sick to the square. Now think of someone you'd carry if you could. Someone ill, worn out, in need of healing of any kind. Picture yourself setting their mat down in the square. If you pray, you can bring their need to God by name, the way the villages brought theirs. If you don't pray, hold them in mind, and ask who could help them that you could reach. The bell holds the time.
Wherever he went. Villages, towns and farms bringing their sick to the marketplace, just to touch the fringe of his cloak.
Your line: touch the fringe. Today, carry one person's need somewhere it can be met: to God, if you pray, or to someone who can help. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: Washed hands (Mark 7:1–13)
186.hook: he challenges traditions used to dodge caring for parents
186.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture, while many Protestant churches weigh every tradition against scripture; many Christians read this passage as a call to check their own customs against love of God and neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, wherever he went, the sick were laid in the marketplaces, reaching for his fringe. Your line was touch the fringe. Whose need did you carry? Day one hundred eighty-six.

A new part of Mark begins: chapters seven to nine, and the question underneath all of it is who is this? It opens at a meal. Some Pharisees and teachers of the law have come up from Jerusalem, and they notice that some of Jesus's disciples are eating without first washing their hands in the ritual way. It's not about germs. It's about holiness, the careful washing that set apart an ordinary meal as something done before God. They ask Jesus why his followers don't keep it. And his answer is about something much bigger than hands. Today's word: tradition.
screen: `MARK SEVEN TO NINE BEGINS.` → `A MEAL, AND UNWASHED HANDS.` → `WHY DON'T THEY KEEP IT?`

segments.voice: Mark stops to explain the custom for readers who aren't Jewish: many washed their hands carefully before eating, and washed cups and pots too, keeping the tradition of the elders. It was, and is, a beautiful practice. Many Jews today still wash their hands with a blessing before eating bread. So the question is a fair one. Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah, in the old King James Bible: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." Then he makes his real charge: "laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." And he gives an example. The commandment says honor your father and mother, which included caring for them in old age. But, he says, you've allowed someone to declare their money Corban, dedicated to God, and then use that to refuse their parents any help. A holy word, used as a loophole. Jewish teachers themselves later wrote rules to release vows that hurt parents, so they saw the danger too. Tradition, in Greek paradosis, means what's handed over, passed from hand to hand. Christians have traditions of their own, and they don't all weigh them the same way. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold sacred Tradition alongside scripture as a way God's word is handed on. Many Protestants give scripture the final word over any tradition. But almost every church reads this passage as a warning to itself, not to anyone else: a habit meant to bring you closer to God can end up used to dodge the people God asked you to love.
screen: `THE TRADITION OF THE ELDERS.` · `LIPS NEAR, HEART FAR.` · `CORBAN: A HOLY LOOPHOLE.` · `PARADOSIS — WHAT'S HANDED ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one habit against its purpose. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you do regularly because it's good. A prayer routine, if you pray. A family ritual. Going to the gym. A rule you keep at work. Ask: what was this for, in the first place? Then ask, honestly: has it ever become a reason to avoid something, or someone? Don't judge yourself. Just look. If you pray, you can ask God to keep the heart of it alive in you. The bell holds the time.
Tradition. From the Greek paradosis, what's handed on. A gift, unless it's used to dodge the love it was meant to carry.
Your line: keep the heart of it. Today, pick one habit and do it for the reason it began, and if it's been an excuse, let it go. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: What comes out (Mark 7:14–23)
187.hook: it's not what goes in that defiles, but what comes out of the heart
187.howItsDone: Most Christians do not keep the Torah's food laws, often citing this passage, and many practice an examination of conscience or reflection at the end of the day, looking back over what they said and did.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tradition, what's handed on, and a holy word used as a loophole. Your line was keep the heart of it. Which habit did you check? Day one hundred eighty-seven.

You've probably had this day. You eat well, you drink your water, you take your vitamins. And then someone cuts you off in traffic, or a coworker takes credit for your work, and what comes out of your mouth is something you'd never want your grandmother to hear. Everything you put in was careful. What came out wasn't. After the argument about washed hands, Jesus calls the whole crowd back to him and says, listen, all of you, and understand. Then he says something so short it sounds like a riddle. Today: what comes out.
screen: `CAREFUL ABOUT WHAT GOES IN.` → `THEN SOMEONE CUTS YOU OFF.` → `LISTEN, ALL OF YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the riddle, in the old King James Bible: "There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man." Defile, in Greek, is a word that means to make common, to make something ordinary that was meant to be set apart. Later, indoors, the disciples ask him about it, and he's a bit exasperated again: "Are ye so without understanding also?" Food goes into the stomach, he says, not into the heart, and then out again. But "from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts," and he names a long list: theft, greed, deceit, envy, arrogance, cruelty. That's what really makes a person unclean. Mark adds a short note of his own here, which many Christians read as Jesus declaring all foods clean. It's one reason most churches don't keep the food laws of the Torah. Jews who keep kosher understand those laws as God's commandments to Israel, and keep them with devotion; and scholars differ on how much Mark's note meant at the time. What almost everyone agrees on is the center of the teaching: the heart. In the Bible, the heart isn't only feelings. It's where you think, decide and choose. It's the kitchen where words get cooked before they're served. So Jesus moves the question from the plate to the source. Not only, what did I take in today? But, what came out?
screen: `NOTHING FROM WITHOUT CAN DEFILE.` · `DEFILE — TO MAKE COMMON.` · `OUT OF THE HEART PROCEED.` · `THE HEART: WHERE YOU CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch what comes out of your mouth. Settle, and breathe. Replay the last day. Not what you ate or watched. What you said. The kind words. The sharp ones. The joke at someone's expense. The complaint you repeated. Don't punish yourself. Just notice where each one came from: tired, scared, jealous, generous, glad. If you pray, you can ask God for a clean heart. If not, just choose one word you'd like to say more of today. The bell holds the time.
What comes out. Jesus's short riddle: it's not what goes in that makes a person unclean, but what comes out of the heart.
Your line: from the heart. Today, before one sharp word leaves your mouth, pause, and ask where it's coming from. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

188.title: Crumbs under the table (Mark 7:24–30)
188.hook: a Syrophoenician mother talks back to Jesus and wins
188.carry: even the dogs eat the crumbs
188.howItsDone: Many Christians look to the Syrophoenician woman as a model of bold, persistent prayer for others, and churches often read her story when speaking about welcome for outsiders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what comes out: not what goes in, but what comes from the heart. Your line was from the heart. Did you catch a sharp word before it left? Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Jesus leaves Galilee and goes north, over the border, into the region of Tyre, a Gentile city on the coast. He slips into a house and wants nobody to know he's there. He's tired. It doesn't work. A woman finds him. She isn't Jewish, she isn't from his people, and she has no claim on him at all. But her little daughter is sick, possessed, Mark says, and she falls at his feet and begs. Any parent knows that kind of begging. And what happens next is one of the most uncomfortable, and most loved, conversations in the Gospels. Today: crumbs under the table.
screen: `NORTH, OVER THE BORDER.` → `A HOUSE, AND NO ONE TO KNOW.` → `A MOTHER AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Mark tells us exactly who she is: "The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation." Greek-speaking, from the Phoenician coast of Syria. An outsider, in every way that mattered then. And Jesus's answer, in the old King James Bible, is hard to hear: "Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs." The children are Israel. The dogs are everyone else. The word he uses means little dogs, house dogs, but it still stings. And she doesn't walk away. She doesn't argue that she isn't one. She picks up his picture and turns it: "Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs." Fine. Then I'll take the crumbs. Anyone who's watched kids eat knows the dog under the table eats well. And Jesus says, for that answer, go home: the demon has left your daughter. She goes home and finds the child lying in bed, well. Christians read this conversation in several ways, and have for centuries. Some say Jesus was testing her faith, and she passed. Some say he was voicing what people around him thought, so that her answer would overturn it. Others say plainly that she changed his mind, and that Mark lets us see it. What all of them notice: she's the one person in Mark who wins an argument with Jesus. And notice the word first. Children first, not children only. Right after this, Jesus heads into more Gentile country. The crumbs, it turns out, are about to become a feast.
screen: `A GREEK, A SYROPHOENICIAN.` · `THE CHILDREN'S BREAD, AND THE DOGS.` · `YET THE DOGS EAT THE CRUMBS.` · `CHILDREN FIRST, NOT ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand up for someone you love. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love who needs something they can't ask for themselves. A child who needs help at school. A parent navigating doctors. A friend facing a system that keeps saying no. Picture yourself, like this mother, refusing to take the first no as the last word. Respectful, clever, stubborn. What would you say? If you pray, you can bring their need to God as boldly as she did. The bell holds the time.
Crumbs under the table. An outsider mother's reply to Jesus, turning his own picture into a yes for her daughter.
Your line: even the dogs eat the crumbs. Today, don't take the first no for someone you love. Ask again, kindly and cleverly. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

189.title: Be opened (Mark 7:31–37)
189.hook: he puts fingers in a deaf man's ears, sighs, and says ephphatha
189.howItsDone: In the Catholic rite of baptism, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they will hear and proclaim God's word; many Christians pray the word for open ears and hearts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, crumbs under the table: a mother who wouldn't take no, and won. Your line was even the dogs eat the crumbs. Who did you ask again for? Day one hundred eighty-nine. Twenty-seven weeks.

Jesus takes the long way back. From Tyre up to Sidon, then all the way around to the east side of the Sea of Galilee, through the ten cities, the Decapolis, where the man called Legion went home to tell his story. Maybe that's why people there bring someone to him. A man who is deaf and can hardly speak. And they beg Jesus to lay his hand on him. What Jesus does next is so physical, so hands-on, that some readers find it almost awkward. Mark keeps every gesture. And one Aramaic word. Today's word: ephphatha.
screen: `THE LONG WAY AROUND.` → `BACK IN THE TEN CITIES.` → `A MAN WHO CANNOT HEAR.`

segments.voice: First, Jesus takes the man aside, away from the crowd. No show. Just the two of them. Then he speaks the man's language, the language of touch. He puts his fingers in the man's ears. He spits and touches his tongue. Then, in the old King James Bible, "looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened." He sighed. A groan, a deep breath out. Mark doesn't explain it. Some hear compassion, some hear prayer, some hear grief at all the ways the world is closed. Ephphatha is Aramaic again, like talitha koum, and Mark translates: be opened. "And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain." The crowd can't keep quiet about it: "He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak." Dumb here is the old word for unable to speak. Anyone who knew the prophet Isaiah would hear his promise that one day the ears of the deaf would be unstopped and the tongue of the mute would sing. And the word lives on in church. In the Catholic baptism rite, the priest may touch the ears and mouth of the newly baptized and say ephphatha, praying that they'll soon hear God's word and speak it. That closes a week. Sheep without a shepherd. It is I. Wherever he went. Tradition. What comes out. Crumbs under the table. And one word, sighed toward heaven: be opened.
screen: `TAKEN ASIDE, AWAY FROM THE CROWD.` · `FINGERS, SPIT AND A SIGH.` · `EPHPHATHA — BE OPENED.` · `HE HATH DONE ALL THINGS WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a sound you usually ignore. Settle, and let your eyes close. Let the obvious sounds come first, and let them pass. Then go looking for the hidden ones. The hum of a machine. Your own heartbeat. Wind against a window. A bird far off. Pick one, and give it your full attention, as if you'd never heard it before. Let your ears be opened. If you pray, you can offer the word to God: ephphatha. The bell holds the time.
Ephphatha. Aramaic for be opened, sighed by Jesus with his fingers in a deaf man's ears.
Your line: be opened. Today, when you notice yourself closing up to a person or an idea, whisper it, and listen one moment longer. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

fork.setup: a crowd brings you a man who can't hear, and begs you to lay your hand on him. what does Jesus do first?
options: lay a hand on his head in front of everyone.
take him aside, alone.
tell him to go and wash.
fork.reveal: he takes him aside from the crowd, touches his ears and tongue, looks up, sighs, and says ephphatha: be opened.

original.note: Aramaic, written in Greek letters by Mark: be opened.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange, magic-sounding word.
what it means: be opened, said privately to a deaf man, with touch, a sigh and a look toward heaven.
what a scholar hears: Aramaic kept in Mark's Greek, an echo of Isaiah 35, and a word still spoken in the Catholic rite of baptism.
